bibl.title: Separate body- and world-referenced representations of visual space in parietal cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Here we report that modulations of visual signals (gain fields) in two adjacent cortical fields, LIP and 7a, are referenced to the body and to the world, respectively.

span.label: spatial reference frames in posterior parietal cortex
span.quote: Head position can be referenced to either the body or to the world.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We recorded from 288 cells in two macaques.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Segregating body- and world-referenced signals into distinct cortical areas keeps the number of variables any one cell population must encode small, raising computational efficiency and avoiding the curse of dimensionality
span.quote: Segregation in the cortex may reflect different computational constraints on information processing, and may thereby increase computational efficiency and help avoid the ‘curse of dimensionality’ that results when attempting to code many M variables within a single group of cells.

span.label: An efference-copy contribution during the passive body-under-head rotation cannot be formally excluded.
span.quote: Equal contributions from efference copy signals under both conditions cannot be ruled out, because it is possible (although unlikely) that the animal actively assisted during the body-underhead movement.

span.label: The extra 7a modulation during active head movement may reflect rotation speed rather than proprioception or efference copy.
span.quote: Alternatively, the faster speed of head rotation in the active head rotation task might have produced a more robust vestibular signal.

span.label: The anatomical source of the vestibular input to 7a is not established by these data.
span.quote: In the absence of direct connections with the brainstem vestibular nuclei, the origin of this input could be either cortical or subcortical from vestibular-related areas.

span.label: The dissociation is near-complete rather than complete, and the exceptions are counted.
span.quote: Out of 31 7a and 59 LIP cells tested, only two cells showed significant effects in both reference frames

span.label: the null for passive body rotation - BOUNDED IN ITS OWN SENTENCE: no effect was found when the body was rotated under a stationary head, and the authors state in the same sentence that proprioceptive or efference-copy signals might still influence 7a cells if delivered together with a vestibular signal, so the null covers one delivery condition and not the mechanism
span.quote: Although we found no effect of passive rotation of the body under the head, it is possible that proprioceptive or efference copy signals might nonetheless influence 7a cells when delivered in conjunction with a vestibular signal

span.label: the dissociation - COUNTED, NOT ASSERTED: of 90 cells tested across the two areas, two showed significant effects in both reference frames, so the separation is reported with the size of its own exception rather than as a clean division
span.quote: Out of 31 7a and 59 LIP cells tested, only two cells showed significant effects in both reference frames

span.label: world-referenced modulation - A FREQUENCY DIFFERENCE BETWEEN AREAS, NOT A PRESENCE/ABSENCE ONE: it was more than twice as frequent in 7a as in LIP, which is a difference of degree between two populations and not a property one area has and the other lacks
span.quote: world-referenced modulation was more than twice as frequent in 7a than in LIP

span.label: extends → earlier parietal gain-field studies, cited only by number as refs 4 and 8
span.quote: However, previous studies have not distinguished between world-referenced and body-referenced signals4,8.

span.label: passive rotation —causes→ 7a
span.quote: Although we found no effect of passive rotation of the body under the head, it is possible that proprioceptive or efference copy signals might nonetheless influence 7a cells when delivered in conjunction with a vestibular signal

span.label: 7a —contrasted-with→ LIP
span.quote: world-referenced modulation was more than twice as frequent in 7a than in LIP

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The absolute value of the gain field is shown for cells whose responses during and immediately after visual cue presentation depended on either bodyor worldreferenced head position (Student’s t-test, P , 0:05; 33 of 90 cells).

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: The distribution of cells with significant effects as a function of anatomical area was statistically significant (chi-squared test on body-referenced modulation: x2 ¼ 9:09; 1; P ¼ 0:0026; chi-squared test on worldreferenced modulation, with Yates’ correction: x2 ¼ 12:271; 1; P ¼ 0:00046).

span.label: regression
span.quote: Gain fields were calculated by fitting a least-squares regression to spike rate.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: the mean absolute modulation in cells with significant effects was approximately 50% greater in 7a than in LIP (1:71 6 0:17 versus 1:11 6 0:13% modulation per degree of head rotation, mean 6 1 s:e:m:)

span.label: Visual gain-field modulation in the two adjacent parietal areas is referenced to different frames: LIP gain fields are body-referenced and 7a gain fields are world-referenced.
span.quote: Here we report that modulations of visual signals (gain fields) in two adjacent cortical fields, LIP and 7a, are referenced to the body and to the world, respectively.

span.label: In LIP, 22 of 59 cells were significantly modulated and almost all of them (20) were body-referenced, with only one world-referenced and one mixed.
span.quote: In cortical area LIP, 22 of 59 cells showed significant (P , 0:05) modulation for at least one of the two rotations: 20 body-referenced, one worldreferenced, and only one mixed bodyand world-referenced.

span.label: In area 7a the pattern reversed: of 11 significantly modulated cells, nine were world-referenced, one body-referenced and one mixed.
span.quote: In area 7a, 11 of 31 cells showed significant modulation: nine worldreferenced, one body-referenced, and one mixed.

span.label: The two reference frames are carried by separate cell populations rather than coexisting on the same cells, since only two of the 90 cells tested showed significant modulation in both frames.
span.quote: Out of 31 7a and 59 LIP cells tested, only two cells showed significant effects in both reference frames.

span.label: World-referenced modulation was both more frequent (40% vs 18% of cells) and about 50% stronger in 7a than in LIP.
span.quote: In a separate series of experiments in which only head-plus-body rotation was performed (see Table 1), world-referenced modulation was more than twice as frequent in 7a than in LIP (40% versus 18% of cells, respectively)

span.label: In 7a, world-referenced signals explained only part of the gain-field modulation produced by active head rotation, unlike in LIP where body-referenced signals accounted for it entirely.
span.quote: Worldreferenced signals account for only part of the effect during active head rotation (Fig. 3).

span.label: Eighteen of the 57 modulated 7a cells were modulated after active head rotation but not after passive body-plus-head rotation, pointing to an additional proprioceptive or efference-copy contribution.
span.quote: Of these 57 cells, 18 showed significant modulation after active head but not after passive body-plus-head rotation, suggesting an influence of proprioception or efference copy.

span.label: World-referenced gain fields in 7a appeared only after rotations fast enough to exceed the vestibular threshold, in six of seven cells tested, identifying the signal source as vestibular.
span.quote: In six of seven cells, gain fields appeared after rotation above but not below threshold, strongly suggesting a vestibular input.

span.label: The authors conclude that posterior parietal cortex segregates spatial information according to the behavioural function it will serve (gaze control versus navigation) rather than by sensory modality.
span.quote: We propose that, in posterior parietal cortex, information is segregated based on the specific functional role it will serve.

span.label: body-under-head rotation
span.quote: To isolate body-referenced gain fields, visual responses to targets presented at identical retinal locations were compared after the body had been counter-rotated underneath the head to one of 2–7 positions (body-under-head rotation); after counter-rotation, the head was always at the same angle with respect to the world, but at different angles with respect to the body.

span.label: body-plus-head rotation
span.quote: To isolate world-referenced gain fields, responses to retinally identical targets were compared after the head and body had been rotated together to one of the same 2–7 positions (body-plus-head rotation); after combined rotation, the head was always at the same angle (08) with respect to the body, but was at varying angles with respect to the world.

span.label: head and body posture (rotation condition)
span.quote: Responses to retinally identical targets were compared on interleaved trials following different head and body movements.

span.label: gain field (percentage change in spike rate per degree)
span.term: gain field (percentage change in spike rate per degree)
span.quote: Gain fields were calculated by fitting a least-squares regression to spike rate.

span.label: retinotopic target location
span.quote: Every trial began with an interval of central fixation followed by a peripheral target, always at the same retinotopic position.

span.label: 288 — total cells recorded, across two macaque monkeys
span.quote: We recorded from 288 cells in two macaques.

span.label: four hemispheres of two adult male rhesus macaque monkeys — the recording sample
span.quote: Data were recorded from four hemispheres of two adult male rhesus macaque monkeys.

span.label: 22 of 59 — LIP cells with significant gain-field modulation in at least one rotation condition
span.quote: In cortical area LIP, 22 of 59 cells showed significant (P , 0:05) modulation for at least one of the two rotations: 20 body-referenced, one worldreferenced, and only one mixed bodyand world-referenced.

span.label: 40% versus 18% — frequency of world-referenced modulation in 7a versus LIP
span.quote: In a separate series of experiments in which only head-plus-body rotation was performed (see Table 1), world-referenced modulation was more than twice as frequent in 7a than in LIP (40% versus 18% of cells, respectively)

span.label: 0:61 6 0:10 ... r2 ¼ 0:40 — regression coefficient relating 7a body-plus-head gain fields to active-head gain fields, with the residual variance left unexplained
span.quote: Regression analysis revealed a coefficient relating the two gain fields of 0:61 6 0:10, with a large amount of residual variance (r2 ¼ 0:40).

span.label: 57 — 7a cells (of 102 tested) with significant gain fields in at least one condition
span.quote: Of 102 cells tested, 57 showed significant gain fields in at least one condition.

span.label: six of seven — cells whose gain fields appeared only after suprathreshold vestibular rotation
span.quote: In six of seven cells, gain fields appeared after rotation above but not below threshold, strongly suggesting a vestibular input.
